why: It sets out, part by part, where things stood in a yamen of any rank - the six rooms two bays each flanking the path to the great hall, the screen wall facing the gate across the street - and says the ranks differed in area but shared the layout. It names the Ming Zhusi zhizhang and Ming huidian, but its shrine list comes from the Qing huidian, and most of that list is the city's altars; the shrines inside the yamen are a shorter list. It hedges the two bays per room as "generally" and says some yamen added more rooms. It also contradicts itself on the west side's order: one sentence gives north to south as war, punishments, works, and the next gives south to north as works, war, punishments. The west-side order has to be confirmed from a closer source.

It names, street by street, which ministries stood east of the gate and which west, which is how the record can say that five ministries stood together and Justice stood apart with the courts. It cites no source for its list of offices and gives no sizes. Its east-side row of five ministries holds for both dynasties. Its west-side list (Imperial Equipage, Sacrifices, Censorate, Justice, Judicial Review) is the Qing arrangement: in the Ming that side held a chief military commission, the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, the Office of Transmission and the Embroidered Uniform Guard. The three judicial offices then stood farther west in the city; the Qing built its Ministry of Justice on the Guard's old site (《日下旧闻考》). So Justice standing apart holds for both dynasties, but where the page puts it is Qing only. It describes one imperial capital, not a provincial seat.

It shows what a ministry held inside - fourteen bureaus by province - and which of its functions (the treasuries, the granaries, the mint) were separate offices of their own. Its only references are the 1989 Cihai (for the Tang renaming) and the Yoro code (for Japan), so the bureaus and the separate offices it lists carry no citation of their own. It runs the Ming and the Qing together - the fourteen provincial bureaus are the Qing count (its own Ming table lists thirteen, with no Jiangnan bureau), and the mint board and the three treasuries are named in their Qing forms. The bureaus sat in the capital and divided the empire's accounts by province; a provincial office was a different body, reached here only by scaling down.

It is a domain's jail described as a place: two separate compounds on confiscated retainers' residence plots, one for samurai (the Noyama jail, twelve cells in two facing rows of six, with an inspection hut and an execution ground) and one for everyone else (the Iwakura jail). Its one cited source, a Kyōhō-era account of Hagi printed in 1891, supports only how the two jails came to stand on the two confiscated plots, and the cell layout, inspection hut and execution ground are uncited. The jails stood apart because two residences were confiscated after one assault in 1645, not by any stated rule, and the article does not say where the magistracy stood; that the jail stood apart from it is our inference. It gives no area.

It says every prefecture, department and county kept a jail, and that from the prefecture up the jail had its own office - the tier at which a jail becomes an institution with a staff. Nothing it cites carries this claim: its one footnote quotes the Ming History on jail abuses. The primary source for the claim is the Ming History's treatise on offices (Mingshi, juan 75, on Wikisource), which lists a jail office with one warden under each prefecture and none under a department or county. The article names the Qing warden's staff (one clerk, two runners, a few menials and guards) but says nothing of the jail's size or place.

It names the five works and the Liulichang's job of firing tile and vessels for the court, which is what our capital's fringe tile works is modeled on. It describes the imperial capital, whose Ministry-of-Works establishments and gate-signal apparatus a provincial seat had no counterpart of, so the form is stepped down two tiers by us. Its period phrase is quoted with no source named.

It describes the plan of Edo's North town magistracy as it stood in 1841 - office on one side, residence on the other, the court with its temporary jail in the widest quarter - and says the South office was built nearly alike. The post does not say which archive or book its plan drawing comes from; that plan, and one of the South office, are linked from the page. It is the magistracy of the shogun's capital, a city of about a million, so it shows the office at its largest and does not give the size of a provincial town's.

It documents the job our bell-and-drum tower is drawn for - sounding the hour the gates shut and open. Its limit is that it speaks of the city gates, not the lane palings. And it describes the imperial capital, whose Ministry-of-Works establishments and gate-signal apparatus a provincial seat had no counterpart of, so the form is stepped down two tiers by us.

It is the historical counterpart of the setting's re-allotment of the village fields: a village re-allotting its land to even out the tax burden and the quality of the soil. The counterpart is not exact. One entry on the page says the re-allotment was made by the agreement of the farmers of one or several villages, and that it redivided the land they already held. It was not common land handed out by a headman. It says the custom was practiced where production was unstable, such as land damaged by rivers - so it was a regional practice, not the general Edo-period tenure, where a household kept the same fields from year to year. Another entry on the page does note that Satsuma domain enforced a re-allotment (kadowari) across the whole domain. The page gives no term or share size.

It states the general purpose of a post town's masugata - defense, making the town hard for an enemy to enter - and shows one surviving example on the ground. It describes a single town; how many post towns had one is not on it.

It gives the measured footprint of the keep, from the castle's own custodians on their own building. The standing building is the three-story turret of 1810, a deliberately modest late-Edo structure, not the five-story keep of 1611 that burned in 1627.

It gives the block and lot dimensions of a planned Edo commoner district, the measure against which a town block's depth can be read. It describes the shogun's capital, not a provincial town, and one district of it; and its picture of small alleys between shops 3 to 5 ken in frontage is offered as a scene to imagine, not as a measured record (the 3 to 5 ken is the shops' frontage; the column gives no width for the alleys). The square block with its open middle is the plan of 1603: after the Meireki fire of 1657, new streets were cut between the blocks and the lots' interiors changed, so it is the early-Edo form.

It gives the dimensions of the most important timber bridge of the shogun's capital, which bounds the width of a town's chief bridge. It does not bound length, which follows the river and not the rank of the place: Edo's Ryōgoku bridge was 94 ken (about 170 m), and the Tōkaidō's Yahagi bridge at the castle town of Okazaki was 208 ken (about 380 m). It is the exceptional bridge of the largest city, not a town's. The figure rests on the one period account it quotes, which is what carries the number.

It describes a real Chinese market town - the tier the setting's towns sit at - with its street plan and its bridges, in the wet rice south. It is one town, a water town in which the canals do much of what streets do elsewhere; it gives no bridge count or dimensions.

It states that the shogunate established and kept tree avenues along the Five Highways and other main roads, which bears on what lined a trunk road near a town. The Nikko avenue itself is an exceptional memorial planting; the article does not say how continuous the ordinary highway avenues were, or how far from a town they ran. Its one sentence on the shogunate's avenues cites a popular trivia paperback (ロム・インターナショナル編『道路地図 びっくり!博学知識』, 2005), so it carries only that such avenues existed, not their extent or when they were ordered; a dictionary entry on 並木 (Kotobank) that dates the order to 1604 would be the closer source. It describes Edo Japan only, standing in for the setting's Chinese side.

It gives the castle's original area, against which the keep's footprint is measured on this page. A 47,000-koku domain is a modest one, which makes it a good anchor; but the English article on the same castle, registered separately, quotes the same extent, so the two keys are one datum in two languages and do not corroborate one another.

It names the usual one-row, three-room plan of a Kyoto townhouse and what each room was for. It describes surviving Kyoto houses (the two it sends readers to are one of early Shōwa and one over a century old), not provincial towns or a dated era, and says itself that the plan changed over time, and gives no sizes beyond the light garden of about one tsubo.

It gives measured sizes for a rural warrior's moated residence, the physical anchor for a samurai house standing among its own fields. The page itself says these were the seats of powerful local clan heads who commanded bands of warriors, built on a scale not seen before. So the 62 by 80 m moat is an upper bound for a great local house, not the size of an ordinary warrior's home, and by the Edo period most samurai lived in castle towns rather than on their lands. It names an excavation only for the Iguchi site. It covers a few sites in one prefecture, medieval rather than Edo-period, and says little of what stood inside; the second size is hedged as an estimate. Updated 2021.

It says what a lord's suburban estate was for and what it held - gardens for leisure, vegetable gardens and bamboo groves supplying the main residence - and that lords and upper retainers kept such houses in other castle towns too. The entries give no size for an estate; they describe daimyo estates at Edo, far larger households than a single samurai's. Outside Edo the Yamakawa entry names the castle-town case only as something found. The Nihon Rekishi Chimei Taikei entry gives one: a street of samurai houses at Sumoto called Shimoyashiki, three ken wide and 237 ken long, lined on both sides by the Inada house's lower residence and its retainers' houses. It does not say what those held.

It lays out the school's martial wing - three halls by art and a bout ground in the south garden - the plan of a large domain's state martial institution. The Kodokan's grounds, about 105,000 square meters, were the largest of any domain school in the country, so it is the top of the range, not the typical case; its martial halls burned in 1868 and the article gives no sizes for them. The paragraph laying out its wings ends on a citation of Suzuki Eiichi's short history of the Mito Kodokan, and it carries the arrangement of the martial wing, not any measure of it.

It names the two kinds of Ming inn a reader would meet - the eating house with lodgers behind, and the cheap "mule-and-horse" inn (骡马大店) in the open country, where men who came driving carts cooked for themselves. It gives no plan and no size, and runs over two thousand years in a few pages.
It gives the assessed yield of the domain whose castle is one of this page's scale anchors, and it dates that figure to the Ikeda enfeoffment so the anchor is not read as the domain's later size.

It states the Chinese pawnshop's building form, the other half of the Japanese storehouse. Its limits are that the sentence on the building, though it gives no period itself, rests on a single footnote to the Macau Museum's page on the Tak Seng On pawnshop (德成按, opened 1917), so the storied pawnshop it describes is the south-China (Macau and Guangdong) pawn tower of the late Qing and Republican trade - one twentieth-century building standing for the type - and it cannot carry the form of a Song, Yuan or Ming pawnshop, which needs another source.

It states how the Heian-kyo block was divided in practice, from mansions to commoner lots. Its Heian sentence has no footnote of its own, so it is used for the kinds of division and not for any size or count. Its sentence on Kyoto's early twentieth-century land readjustment, which treated both sides of a street as one ward, describes a modern scheme and is not used; the medieval both-sided ward (ryogawa-machi) that scheme inherited is a separate, pre-modern statement in the article.
It places the castle on its promontory between the rivers and the bay, the flank position with water on two sides that this page cites it for.

It gives the Edo block in figures, the Japanese early-modern counterpart of the ancient capital's block. It describes the one quarter it is about rather than all of Edo, and it says itself that the use of the open middle is unknown. Its figures are for the plan as first laid out in 1603: the column also says that after the Meireki fire of 1657 new streets were cut through these blocks and their insides were rearranged, so the square block with its open middle is the early form, not the one this quarter kept for the rest of the Edo period.

It gives the great merchant's site area and frontage, which the official record does not; its storehouse areas repeat the national designation record, which Bunka-cho's Cultural Heritage Online publishes and which is the better citation for them. The storehouses were built before 1822, but the main house whose frontage and floor area it gives was raised in 1870, just after the Edo period, rebuilt after the 1864 fire in the old form. Its site area of about 1,200 square meters disagrees with another page's 30 by 52 m, and it reports the storehouses' surviving the 1864 fire as what is said.

A second, independent statement of the site's size and the storehouses' place. Its 30 by 52 m does not agree with the 1,200 square meters given elsewhere; which is right is not settled here. The present main house was built in 1870, after the fire of 1864, so it is early Meiji work in an Edo-period form, on a plot the family has held since 1764. By the register's own account it is among the largest townhouses in Kyoto, so its frontage and depth are those of a great merchant house, not of an ordinary townhouse.

It gives Kitsuki's sandwich plan - warriors on the heights, merchants below - which is the arrangement this page cites the town for. The page itself calls the arrangement unique to Kitsuki among castle towns, so the form is cited as one attested case and not as a norm.

It defines the masugata, its inner and outer forms and its two gates, which is what a Japanese-model gate court is drawn from. It gives no dimensions, and its account of where each form developed is marked as wanting a source.
It states the domain granary's two-way job - tax rice in, stipends out - which is the whole function of the granary district on our capital.
It adds one thing the encyclopedia does not: that a causeway across a wet moat could hold the water at a different level on each side.
